Key Finding
A clear multi-year decline in activity is evident: average daily steps fell by 692 from 2015 (10963) to 2025 (10271). The peak year was 2016 at 11105 steps/day, and the lowest was 2018 at 10003 steps/day. Seasonally, December is the most active month (11113 avg steps) while January is the least (10176 avg steps) — a post-holiday recovery pattern. Workout participation fluctuates but has actually slightly increased (+1.2pp over the decade), suggesting users are doing fewer steps overall but are marginally more likely to log a structured workout.
Section 06

Key Insights & Recommendations

Synthesize the most important findings from the analysis and provide data-driven recommendations for product and engagement strategies.

High Priority
Address the Decade-Long Activity Decline

Average daily steps declined by 692 steps from 2015 to 2025, with 2016 being the peak year (11105) and 2018 the lowest (10003). This is not explained by seasonal variation — it is a structural trend. However, workout participation has slightly increased (+1.2pp), suggesting users may be shifting from incidental activity (walking, transit) to structured workouts.


Recommendation: Introduce a "Daily Movement Goal" feature that bridges structured workouts with incidental activity. In-app prompts timed to low-activity periods (Thursday is the lowest step day at 10317 avg) could help recover lost incidental activity.

High Priority
January Recovery Campaign — capitalize on the December Peak

December is the highest-step month (11113 avg steps) while January is the lowest (10176), a swing of 937 steps. Users appear highly active in December (holiday season, end-of-year goals) then sharply drop in January — the classic "resolution" gap.


Recommendation: Pre-schedule a "New Year Reset" engagement campaign launching January 2nd. Provide personalized step goals derived from December's baseline, and pair with sleep and hydration tracking to address the Tired-mood cluster observed in January data.

Medium Priority
Target the "Tired" User Segment for Workout Engagement

"Tired" users (1,329 records, 33.2% of all days) show the highest stress (5.58), lowest sleep (6.95h), and yet have the highest average steps (10749). They are active but unwell — a group that may benefit from stress-reducing workout formats.


Recommendation: Introduce a "Yoga & Recovery" or "Low-Stress Workout" tracking category specifically targeting the Tired segment.推送 low-intensity workout suggestions on days when stress is elevated and sleep was below average. Consider a "wellness score" composite metric combining these signals.

Medium Priority
Leverage Gender-Parity in Workout Participation

Workout participation rates are nearly equal across genders (83.6% male vs. 82.7% female), but workout type preferences may differ. Gym is the most common workout type overall (689 records), while Yoga and Walking also have significant shares.


Recommendation: Since participation is gender-equitable, focus personalization on workout type recommendations. Analyze which workout types yield highest calorie burn per minute for each gender (Running leads for both at ~622 kcal/day avg) and promote accordingly.

Medium Priority
Hydration Tracking as an Engagement Hook

Water intake averages 2.49L/day across the cohort, with a wide range (0.5–5.0L). Hydration tracking is currently passive — users who do track water may have different engagement profiles. Correlating water intake with step counts and workout type could surface "healthy behavior clusters."


Recommendation: Introduce a hydration reminder feature triggered after workout completion. Users who complete a workout and log water intake simultaneously represent a high-engagement cohort — target them for advanced wellness features (stress tracking, sleep coaching).
